stops.segment: The Piedmontese Beginning
stops.stop: Turin, the letter to Euler
stops.date_confidence: MacTutor dates the letter 12 August 1755 and attests both the tautochrone results and the new method of maxima and minima. Location inferred: every source has him resident in Turin through 1755. The further detail that Euler held back his own work on the subject so that Lagrange could publish first is standard in the literature but was not verified against a source in this pass. The Euler Archive correspondence guide cited in the research dossier returned 404 when checked and is recorded here as unreachable rather than as support.

stops.segment: The Terror
stops.stop: Place de la Revolution, Lavoisier's head
stops.date_confidence: the execution is dated 8 May 1794. Whether Lagrange was present is not established by any source reached, and the stop is pinned at the scaffold because that is where the event happened, not because his attendance is attested. The remark is the most repeated sentence anyone ever put in his mouth and its exact French wording and first documentary appearance have not been traced; a variant reading runs 'cut off that head, but France may not produce another like it in a century'. Coordinates inherited byte-identical from louis_xvi.journey.json, which pins the Place de la Revolution at 48.8648, 2.3268.

stops.segment: The Schools of the Republic
stops.stop: Paris, the Bureau des longitudes and the new Institut
stops.date_confidence: fr.wikipedia, 'Bureau des longitudes': created by the law of 25 June 1795 and first convened on 6 July 1795 in a room of the Petit Luxembourg, with Lagrange a founding member as geometre and its second president from September 1795. Membership of the mathematical class of the Institut national, founded the same year in the Louvre, is folded into this stop; its month is not established here.
